B15_00: Before mitosis the Golgi is disassembled so its stacks can be partitioned between daughter cells, and its fragmentation can act as a checkpoint for mitotic entry. CDK1, polo-like and VRK kinases phosphorylate GM130 (GOLGA2), syntaxin 5 and GBF1, breaking golgin tethers and halting vesicle fusion so the ribbon disperses into tubules and vesicles, linking cell cycle control to Golgi inheritance.
B15_01: Schwann cells must maintain mature peripheral myelin so internodes stay compact and conduction stays fast; failure causes demyelinating neuropathies such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease. Periaxin anchors the membrane to basal lamina via dystroglycan, SH3TC2 and NDRG1 handle trafficking, plectin links the cytoskeleton, fatty acid 2-hydroxylase supplies hydroxylated sphingolipids, and Akt signalling sustains renewal and axonal support.
B15_02: Regulation of Golgi organization sets how compact, positioned and connected the ribbon is, affecting directional secretion, glycosylation and mitotic disassembly. AKAP9 and PDE4DIP anchor Golgi microtubules, CAMSAPs stabilise their minus ends and MYO5A supports positioning; RAB33B and RAB43 direct traffic, STX5 and STX18 maintain cisternal fusion, and ERK signals ribbon severing. Disruption fragments the Golgi and alters cargo and glycans.
B15_03: During apoptosis, phosphatidylserine moves from the inner to the outer plasma membrane leaflet, serving as an eat-me signal for phagocytes; failed clearance causes inflammation and autoimmunity. XKR8, activated by caspase cleavage, and phospholipid scramblases mediate exposure, and calcium entry can cause it non-apoptotically. The process links FAS ligand death signalling to corpse removal and to platelet procoagulant surfaces.
B15_04: Membrane rafts are cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich domains that cluster receptors and signalling enzymes, supporting caveolae, clathrin-independent endocytosis and mechanosensing; caveolin loss causes muscular dystrophy and cardiomyopathy. Caveolins oligomerise to form invaginations, flotillin marks other rafts, and PACSIN2 bends membranes, while integrin-linked kinase, IQGAP1 and matrix contacts coordinate raft organisation with actin and adhesion.
B15_05: After mitosis each daughter cell rebuilds a sealed nuclear envelope; failure leaves leaky nuclei, micronuclei and DNA damage. CHMP7 recruits CHMP4B and ESCRT-III partners to seal holes, recycled by VPS4A and VPS4B, while REEP3 and REEP4 clear ER from chromatin and spastin severs spindle microtubules. BANF1 with ANKLE2 tethers membranes to chromatin, and RCC1 restores the Ran gradient for transport.
B15_06: Mitotic nuclear membrane organization covers envelope breakdown and rebuilding around daughter genomes, restoring compartmentalisation and transport and preventing micronuclei and DNA damage. BAF tethers chromatin to inner membrane proteins under ANKLE2-regulated phosphorylation, VPS4A and BROX help seal gaps, spastin clears trapped microtubules, REEP proteins remove ER from chromatin, and SUMO and RCC1-driven Ran-GTP coordinate timing.
B15_07: After mitosis, Golgi fragments reassemble into stacked cisternae so daughter cells can resume secretion, glycosylation and polarised traffic, as part of organelle inheritance. Membrane fusion is central, with a deubiquitinase reversing p97/VCP-linked ubiquitin marks, and a 14-3-3 adaptor and the CCM3-STK25 module linking Golgi structure to polarity and stress. Loss of the lipid-transfer protein VPS13B causes Cohen syndrome.
B15_08: Tail-anchored proteins have a C-terminal transmembrane segment that emerges only after translation, so they are inserted into the ER post-translationally; substrates include SNAREs, cytochrome b5 and apoptotic regulators. A BAG6-SGTA-UBL4A-GET4 complex shields the tail and loads GET3, which docks at GET1 and CAMLG, while the EMC and MMGT1 insert less hydrophobic tails. Failures cause developmental and neurological problems.
B15_09: Multi-pass membrane proteins such as transporters, channels and GPCRs need each helix inserted into the ER with correct topology. After SEC61 delivers initial segments, a multi-pass translocon including TMCO1-CCDC47 and nicalin-NOMO-TMEM147 integrates the rest and shields them until they pack. Defects cause misfolding, calcium problems and ER stress, and TMCO1 loss causes a skeletal and craniofacial syndrome.
B15_10: Regulation of endosome organization controls endosome maturation, shaping and positioning so cargo reaches lysosomes, recycles or enters autophagy. Contributors include a late-endosomal GTPase licensing lysosome fusion, a lysosomal membrane protein delivering glucocerebrosidase, a phosphoinositide phosphatase, a ubiquitinated-cargo adaptor and a ubiquitin ligase for organelle clearance. Several are mutated in Parkinson disease, reflecting neuronal reliance on endosomal sorting.
B15_11: The peripheral ER forms a polygonal network of tubules that contact mitochondria, endosomes and the plasma membrane for lipid and calcium exchange and extend along axons. Reticulons and hairpin proteins such as ARL6IP1 impose curvature, and atlastin GTPases fuse tubule tips into three-way junctions. Mutations in atlastin-1, reticulon-2 and ARL6IP1 cause hereditary spastic paraplegia.
B15_12: T-tubules carry surface depolarisation deep into striated muscle cells, enabling uniform calcium release and contraction; their loss in heart failure and myopathies weakens contraction. BIN1 forms tubular invaginations, caveolin-3 supplies caveolae, ankyrin-B targets channels, SERCA2 and mitsugumin-29 link the structure to calcium handling, and CSRP3 connects it to sarcomeres, ensuring excitation-contraction coupling.
B15_13: Vesicle fusion at the Golgi delivers cargo and sustains secretion, glycosylation and protein flow from ER to cell surface. A long coiled-coil tether first captures incoming vesicles, then SNAREs zipper into a four-helix bundle to merge bilayers, with distinct SNAREs serving cis-Golgi and trans-Golgi arrival routes; Yip-family proteins support Golgi and ER exit site organisation. Loss collapses the Golgi and blocks secretion.
B15_14: Calcium-activated phosphatidylcholine scrambling lets lipids flip between membrane leaflets when cytosolic calcium rises, also exposing phosphatidylserine for platelet procoagulant activity and engulfment signals. Anoctamins, especially ANO6, act as calcium-dependent scramblases, and ANO6 loss causes the bleeding disorder Scott syndrome; a phospholipid scramblase adds activity. The process links calcium signalling to coagulation, cell clearance and microvesicle shedding.
B15_15: The cornified envelope is the insoluble protein-lipid shell formed by terminally differentiating keratinocytes, creating the skin barrier against water loss, microbes and allergens. Its assembly involves protein crosslinking and lipid delivery, supported by a MAF-family transcription factor, a histone deacetylase, syntaxin-mediated lamellar body secretion, glucosylceramide synthesis and dermokine. Defects cause ichthyosis and the barrier failure of atopic dermatitis.
B15_16: ER positioning determines where lipids and calcium are exchanged and which organelles the ER contacts. Extended synaptotagmins tether cortical ER to the plasma membrane and transfer glycerolipids, GRAMD2A marks distinct contacts, and VAPA and VAPB capture FFAT-motif proteins for sterol, phosphoinositide and calcium exchange. Loss disturbs store-operated calcium entry and lipid balance, and VAPB mutation causes familial motor neuron disease.
B15_17: Endosome membrane tubulation forms tubular extensions that become recycling carriers; without it, receptors and transporters are degraded in lysosomes instead of returning to the surface or Golgi. BAR-domain sorting nexins SNX1 and SNX2 pair with SNX5 or SNX6 to sense curvature and select cargo, TMCC1 acts at ER contacts for fission, and a coronin and a MICAL effector add actin and Rab input.
B15_18: Stop-transfer anchor sequences halt translocation and become stable ER membrane-spanning helices, giving type I and multipass proteins correct topology; otherwise weakly hydrophobic anchors fail and clients are degraded. Most components are subunits of the ER membrane protein complex, an insertase that lowers the cost of inserting weak segments and chaperones their assembly. Their loss reduces levels of many receptors, transporters and channels.
B15_19: Open mitosis requires nuclear envelope breakdown so spindle microtubules can reach chromosomes. CDK1-cyclin, PLK1, NEK6, VRK1 and protein kinase C phosphorylate lamins, pore and inner membrane proteins, dissolving the lamina, while dynein and DCTN1 tear the envelope mechanically. CTDNEP1 and lipin link breakdown to membrane lipid synthesis and to later nuclear reassembly in daughter cells.
B15_20: Oligodendrocytes continuously renew mature CNS myelin to keep axons insulated, conduction fast and fibres metabolically supported; failure causes late-onset demyelination, axonal degeneration and leukodystrophy-like disease. A fatty acid 2-hydroxylase supplies myelin sphingolipids, a myelin transcription factor sustains structural gene expression, a lipid phosphatase restraining PI3K-AKT-mTOR sets sheath thickness, and clusterin adds extracellular chaperone activity.
B15_21: This pathway governs how much tubular ER network a cell builds, which determines organelle contacts and lipid and calcium distribution. Reticulon-like and hairpin proteins such as ARL6IP1 and TMEM33 tune membrane curvature, LNPK stabilises three-way junctions, and RAB3GAP1-RAB3GAP2 links organisation to Rab regulation. Loss causes hereditary spastic paraplegia and Warburg micro syndrome, affecting long axons and neurodevelopment.
B15_22: Integrins link cells to the matrix and transduce adhesive cues, so their production rate governs attachment, migration and remodelling. Upstream regulators here include a TGF-beta family ligand driving fibrotic adhesion programmes, a fibrillar collagen ligand, a NADPH oxidase generating redox signals and a nuclear hormone receptor. Integrin abundance matters in fibrosis, epithelial and endothelial adhesion and tumour invasion.
B15_23: Mammalian Golgi stacks are laterally linked into a pericentrosomal ribbon that supports orderly traffic, uniform glycosylation and polarised secretion and is dismantled at mitosis. Golgins and GRASP tethers such as GOLGA2, TRIP11, GCC2 and GORASP1 bridge cisternae, GOLPH3 with MYO18A applies tension, and VAMP4 and TMED5 contribute fusion and cargo functions. Ribbon fragmentation occurs in neurodegeneration and stress.
B15_24: Multivesicular bodies form when late endosome membrane buds inward, packaging ubiquitinated proteins into intralumenal vesicles for lysosomal degradation or exosome release and permanently silencing activated receptors; failure contributes to tumour growth and neurodegeneration. ESCRT complexes act in order, from HGS-STAM and TSG101 to VPS25-VPS36-SNF8 and CHMP filaments, with VPS4 and VTA1 recycling them; the same machinery serves abscission and viral budding.
B15_25: This pathway regulates membrane tubulation during endocytosis, organelle remodelling and scission, deciding whether vesicles pinch off or tubular carriers persist. Contributors include a BAR-domain curvature protein, a large fission GTPase forming neck collars, an ARF GAP linking shaping to adhesion signalling, an actin nucleation-promoting factor and a lipid-flipping ATPase, integrating lipid composition, actin force and curvature sensing.
B15_26: Cells in mechanically stressed tissues such as muscle must reseal plasma membrane tears within seconds, a repair triggered by calcium influx. Annexin A2 with S100A10 nucleates repair, AHNAK organises the subsarcolemmal complex, myosin-9 draws edges together, and a Rab GTPase with a synaptotagmin-like effector delivers patching vesicles; caspase-7 links severe damage to apoptosis. Impaired repair underlies some muscular dystrophies.
B15_27: Much of the peripheral ER is a network of highly curved tubules where organelle contacts, lipid transfer and calcium handling occur, and which extends as cells grow processes. Reticulons and ARL6IP1 insert wedge-shaped domains to generate curvature at tubules and sheet edges, while protrudin links ER to microtubule-driven extension. Mutations cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, reflecting the dependence of long axons on ER shape.
B15_28: The ER remains one continuous network through homotypic fusion of tubules, allowing contents, calcium and proteins to diffuse and the ER to be remodelled. The atlastins ATL1, ATL2 and ATL3 tether and fuse tubule tips through GTP-driven conformational change, aided by a SNARE-associated factor and a deubiquitinase. ATL1 mutations cause hereditary spastic paraplegia and ATL3 defects cause sensory neuropathy.
B15_29: Endosomes acidify as they mature through proton pumping, which releases receptor ligands, frees iron from transferrin, activates hydrolases and is exploited by viruses and toxins. The vacuolar H+-ATPase, with V0 proton channel and V1 ATPase subunits and assembly factors ATP6AP1, ATP6AP2 and TMEM9, does the pumping, while CLCN3 provides chloride counterion conductance. Acidification also supports secretory vesicles, including FASLG delivery.
